readerTitle: Why the factory that sold to everyone found almost no one
caseNote: 가상 사례 (포장재 공장, 예약 앱) + 실제 기업 (Facebook 초기 확장 경로). 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 좁은 시장은 작은 야망이 아니라, 무엇이 맞는지 가장 빨리 배우고 고객이 다른 고객을 데려오게 만드는 출발점이다.
misconception: 목표 시장이 넓을수록 팔 기회가 많다. 시장을 좁히면 성장이 막힌다.

sources.text: Facebook(당시 Thefacebook)은 2004년 2월 하버드 학생 대상으로 시작해 다른 대학으로, 이후 일반 사용자로 확대 (Meta 공식 연혁)
포장재 공장과 예약 앱 사례, 차트 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Facebook이 2004년 하버드 학생 전용으로 시작해 다른 대학으로 넓힌 뒤 2006년 일반 공개했다는 연혁을 게시 전 Meta 공식 자료로 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why the factory that sold to everyone found almost no one
body: A small factory cuts custom foam inserts that keep products safe inside shipping boxes. Its website says: *Protective packaging for any product.*
In a year it sent hundreds of quotes. Most buyers ordered once, if at all. The owner's plan for next year: reach even more industries.

image.label: A foam insert holding a fragile instrument in a box
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 공장 작업대 위, 열린 상자 안에 정밀 기기 모양에 딱 맞게 파인 폼 인서트. 뒤 벽에는 "For any product"라고 적힌 큰 현수막. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Sales are flat. What next?
body: You're the owner. Customers range from online furniture sellers to toy shops to a few small firms that make lab instruments.
What do you do next year?

options.text: Add more industries to the website and send more quotes
options.feedback: More quotes spread your time thinner. You still won't learn why most buyers never come back.

options.text: Find the customers who keep reordering and build around them
options.feedback: You give up some broad appeal for now. In return you learn exactly what one group needs. That trade is this lesson.

options.text: Cut prices 15% to win more of the quotes you already send
options.feedback: Orders may rise, but buyers who came for price leave just as easily. And it doesn't tell you who really needs you.

cards.title: One group kept coming back.
body: The owner sorted a year of orders by customer type and asked: who reordered within six months?
Lab instrument makers stood out. A cracked instrument can cost thousands, so a perfect insert matters far more to them than to a toy shop.

cards.title: Narrowing your market
body: **Narrowing your market** means choosing a small, specific group whose problem is sharpest, then serving them so well they come back and tell others like them.
A good narrow market is one you can name, find, and that talks to itself. *Small firms shipping fragile lab instruments* passes. *Anyone who ships things* doesn't.
The factory rebuilt around that group: ready-made sizes for common instruments, two-day turnaround, and drop-test reports buyers could show their own customers.

image.label: A wide target shrinking to one bright bullseye
image.brief: 왼쪽에는 흐릿한 큰 원 안에 여러 업종 아이콘(가구, 장난감, 선물, 실험기기)이 흩어져 있고, 오른쪽에는 실험기기 아이콘 하나만 있는 작고 선명한 과녁. 가운데 화살표로 연결.

cards.title: A narrow group makes everything clearer.
body: When customers share one need, four things get easier:
list: **Signals:** a reorder or a lost customer actually tells you something
**Choices:** you know which features to build and which to skip
**Word of mouth:** people in one field talk at trade shows and in forums
**Your message:** one sentence can speak to all of them
cards.callout: Facebook followed this path. In 2004 it opened only to Harvard students, then spread to other colleges, and only later to everyone.

cards.title: Narrow by need, not by label.
body: Age, city or company size are easy cuts, but often the wrong ones. The lab firms weren't alike in size. They shared a problem: fragile, expensive goods in transit.
Narrow is a starting point, not a final address. Once you win one group, move to the next group that shares most of the need. For the factory, that might be medical device repair shops.

cards.title: Narrow can go wrong too.
list: **Too small:** check the group has enough buyers to sustain you, and that they pay
**Wrong group:** pick by behavior, like reorders and use, not by who compliments you most
**Real cost:** for a while you'll underserve other customers, and some revenue may dip
cards.callout: Narrowing is a bet. Make it on evidence.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app.
body: Your scheduling app is built for *any small business*. Signups come from salons, tutors, plumbers and dog groomers.
After three months, groomers are far more likely to still be active users. What do you do?

options.text: Build the top feature each group asks for
options.feedback: Everyone gets a little, no one gets a product that fits. Your roadmap splits four ways.

options.text: Rebuild onboarding, pricing and marketing for dog groomers first
options.feedback: You lose some signups from other groups for now. But you learn fast, and groomers recommend tools to each other.

options.text: Keep the broad pitch and add a landing page for groomers
options.feedback: A cheap test, but the product is still built for everyone. The groomers' edge may never grow.

cards.softwareNote: In software, the best clue for where to narrow is usually retention split by customer type, not total signups.

cards.title: Win one group completely before you chase everyone.
body: A narrow market isn't small ambition. It's the fastest way to learn what fits, and to get customers who bring others like them.
**Try it today:** list your ten most loyal customers by repeat behavior. Write the one problem they share. Can you name that group in five words?
